utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al., thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, 14th of October, 2008. Good morning to the accused, the Defence counsel, the OTP representatives, and all the people helping us. I understood that Mr. Scott wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good morning Mr. President; good morning to each of Your Honours; good morning to counsel and all those in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, in light of some of the events yesterday and some of the directions given by the Chamber, I thought it was appropriate just to make a further record on where some of these matters stand, and I did it specifically out of the hearing of the witness just to try to take it as low key, if you will, as possible and not to involve the witness in these procedural matters unnecessarily. First, Your Honour, as I'm sure you know by now, while the Prosecution -- the Prosecution acknowledges and appreciates receiving a letter late last evening, and let me be very clear about that so no one misses it. The Prosecution appreciates the obvious effort that went into getting us the letter late last night. Now, having said that, the Prosecution, we stand by our position. The Prosecution categorically rejects and will continue to reject any position at getting such a letter at midnight before court at 9.00 a.m. the following day when the summary is six months late cures the problem or somehow shifts the penalty for or the responsibility to deal with that violation to the victim of that violation. That's what people call blaming the victim. Further, the letter in reality provides very little substantive information except to repeat and slightly different ways the same argument Mr. Karnavas has now made ad infinitum and that is that the Prosecution should have known, the Prosecution could have expected, the Prosecution might have guessed. It goes on repeatedly in the letter, and I'll just cite the Chamber to a few examples. On page 2, it was to be understood, a matter which has been covered throughout the trial, he could be expected to testify about, quite naturally by virtue of his position would be expected to know, it is widely known, Mr. Zelenika would be expected to know, someone holding such a position as Mr. Zelenika would be expected to know, as the Prosecution knows, Mr. Zelenika would be expected. That's not a summary. That's same arguments that Mr. Karnavas has been making for some weeks now and which the Prosecution has rejected on every occasion and rejects this morning. That is not a summary, and just so the record is very clear on the future of this issue and unfortunately I predict it may not go away. Had this information, had this letter been provided to us earlier we would not consider this a sufficient summary. It is not a summary required by the Rules. It's just the same letter making the arguments Mr. Karnavas has made over the past weeks. This is not a summary. This is not what 65 ter requires. As I said yesterday and I'm say it again today and I'll say it again tomorrow, if necessary, that argument, the argument that shifts the responsibility on the Prosecution to somehow deal with it is completely false, completely disingenuous and has nothing to do, and I repeat has nothing to do with the other party meeting its obligations under the Rules, and I decline -- the Prosecution, Your Honour, declines the responsibility to take any extraordinary efforts to cure a violation by another party. That is that party's responsibility. That responsibility lies with the other party, and it is up to the Court of course whether it wishes to enforce the Rules or not. Your Honour, in light of the events, in light of the letter last night I wanted to make the Prosecution position very clear. I may try having made that record to be a bit quieter today. Maybe I will succeed, maybe I won't, but I wanted to be very clear on that position, Your Honour. This letter cures nothing. It does not shift any burden onto the Prosecution. The Prosecution position is there is a Rule violation, there continues to be a Rule violation, and the burden does not fall on the Prosecution to fix it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may briefly respond. Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the Trial Chamber believes that this discussion should not continue. You sent this letter as required by the Trial Chamber. Mr. Scott is telling us that he's not satisfied, that the Rules have been violated. You've already heard the view of the Trial Chamber. In the future, I say in the future, you will have to prepare summaries giving the facts that will be underlying the examination-in-chief so that the Prosecutor is in a position to prepare for his cross-examination and for the Rules to apply and to be applied. Everybody knows that, and I think you got the message. Personally, I hate preventing counsel from doing his work. It's not in my nature. I do everything I can to avoid that. In the future, you must make sure that you have comprehensive factual summaries. This is demanded by the Rules. And Mr. Scott is right in asking for the Rules to apply just as much as you are entitled to ask the Prosecutor to provide you with information. This is what you had requested during the Prosecution case. So let's not spend minutes if not hours on this. We have six accused, and they are -- they have been in custody for several years now. They are entitled to a trial that does not last too long. We must make every possible effort for the trial to unfold in good pace whilst safeguarding everybody's rights. Do you want to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just two minutes, Your Honour, just to point out, just to point out that in the letter, we make reference to a decision made by the Trial Chamber back on -- on 20th of May, 2008. I also make reference to Mr. Stringer's letter to us. And contrary to some of the comments that were directed to us by Judge Trechsel, we have made a good faith effort. Perhaps we have fallen short, but we were -- we proceeded with the understanding that what we had provided was sufficient when you consider not just the summary but the paragraphs to the indictment and also the documents that specifically pointed out that we would be using in -- with this particular witness. So it's not somewhat of a fishing expedition. They weren't inundated with a sea of documents. They were specifically notified what documents and from that, they would have been able to glean that this gentleman with his position would be competent to testify about such matters as the payment bureau. That said, I take your -- your instructions, and we will do better, but I certainly wish to under -- underscore, because I think there is the impression, at least I have the perception from comments and the attitudes that have come from certain members of the Bench that we are deliberately obstructing the process and we are conducting ourselves unethically, and if that is the case, then we should perhaps schedule a hearing on an order to show cause on that, because we are entitled to due process. That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for Mr. Coric. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should only like to get an opportunity to say a few words. I don't need more than a couple of minutes. Regarding yesterday's discussion about part of the evidence given in the courtroom by the last witness -- by the current witness on a topic not specifically identified in the 65 ter summary. I remembered and I checked yesterday the transcript of Witness E who testified on the 11th September 2007. The Prosecutor was questioning the witness on Dretelj topics. It is page of the transcript 22085, beginning with line 15, and there is, in fact, no mention of Dretelj either in the summary or in any other notification, and I objected to this questioning because the Defence had not been able to adequately prepare for such examination. On page 22086, lines 1 to 8, we have the decision of the Trial Chamber wherein the Trial Chamber says the witness is competent to witness -- to give evidence on Dretelj camp. It doesn't matter that it's not in the summary, that the Defence should have been prepared for that and to respond adequately. The Trial Chamber can verify what I'm saying. So can Mr. Scott. And I'm saying this only to remind you of the positions taken, because yesterday's topic was analogous, and the Trial Chamber took a completely different stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] good morning. May I also say a few sentences? The Defence of General Petkovic tried yesterday with several witnesses to compare three statements that we have. One is a summary of a statement -- correction, not three statements, three documents. One of the documents is the summary of a statement. The second document is the statement itself, and the third document is testimony. If we compare these three documents, we will see that there are dramatic differences between them. In the summary there is no reference even to whole topics let alone facts related to parts of the statement, whereas testimony contains even more additional topics because the Prosecution used documents to deal with topics that were not covered even by the statement, let alone the summary. We will make a comparative analysis of the evidence given by several randomly chosen witnesses so the Trial Chamber has an opportunity to acquaint themselves with the summaries for these witnesses that were not provided to the Trial Chamber and to show that the Prosecution, when they mention summaries, actually refer to statements prepared for particular witnesses. And I believe this comparative analysis will help us resolve this dilemma concerning summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] thank you, Ms. Alaburic. Let's have the witness brought in, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for the delay. We had to deal with a point of procedure. I hope you had a good evening. And I'll ask Mr. Karnavas to proceed with his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could get the usher to help us out and provide the witness the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to pick up where we left off yesterday at the very same document that we were discussing, 973. We hadn't finished on that document yet. It's the first document on the chapter under "Economy." And in this particular order that's dated 8 May 1992, we see that the municipality was taking certain equipment and availing itself to certain resources from the SDK, the public accounting -- the Public Auditing Service, and the Sarajevo Commercial Bank. At that point in time, can you tell us whether the Yugoslav dinar was circulating in and around Jablanica municipality, and if so, what was its value?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that. The Yugoslav dinar was in circulation, but it had absolutely no market value because you could buy nothing with it and nobody wanted to take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had you -- were you aware at the time how the Public Auditing Service, the SDK, worked?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us whether it was working within the municipality of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDK was not able to operate at all because it had been part of a system of a network which is the social accountancy service at the level of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it had an organisational unit in each municipality, but since the state had broken down in all its aspects, the SDK had also broken down. It was the vehicle of the payment system, and the payment system itself broke down. Payments ceased. All that was left of the SDK in Jablanica was a building in which you could get no business done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday I asked you a question about, if you may recall, in one of the minutes where two individuals from, I believe, the Crisis Staff were to be dispatched to Grude to have some discussions, and I had asked you about how was payment going to take place, and you indicated, as I recall, that it would be some sort of a bartering system. You would give granite or wood, timber, or whatever resources you had in exchange for the services; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about money? What sort of currency was being circulated or being used at the time in Jablanica so that citizens could meet their -- their daily needs?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time we are discussing, the citizens were able to meet their daily needs if they had German Deutschmarks or the Croatian dinar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, where would the Croatian dinar be coming from, or the German marks, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The foreign currency came from the market in the Republic of Croatia. Namely, many businesses in Jablanica had warehouses in the Republic of Croatia from which they traded. They had earlier earned payments due to them from prior businesses, and they had non-residence accounts in various places in the Republic of Croatia from where all this currency arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to speak a little slower. Not too slow, but a little slower. This is to assist our translators, okay?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 00783. We looked at this very briefly, yesterday, but again I just want to point out or have you point out a couple things to us. This is 10 May 1992. It's signed by the president of the Crisis Staff, Hamdo Sefer. Now -- and if we look at the currencies listed, we see the dinar. As I understand it you indicated that would be the Yugoslav dinar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The German mark, and then we see Croatian dinars. And I don't know whether I asked you this yesterday, but was the Bosnian and Herzegovinian dinar in circulation at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not ask me that yesterday, and the BH dinar was not in circulation, and nobody ever saw it in Jablanica during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Why was it necessary to list the fuel prices with -- with German marks or Croatian dinars? Why not just use the Yugoslav dinar?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, you could not buy fuel for the Yugoslav dinar. You could buy it for other currencies that I mentioned -- that are mentioned here. The Yugoslav dinar was indicated just for purposes of comparison. Yugoslav dinars were not in circulation, and you could not buy fuel for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, 1D 00914. Here we have a conclusion by the Crisis Staff. It's signed by President Nijaz Ivkovic. And what national is Mr. Ivkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nijaz Ivkovic is Muslim by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And on -- on that -- at that period of time, we're talking June 1992, the Crisis Staff, could you please give us the breakdown between how many Muslims, how many Serbs, how many Croats on there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you straight away there were no Serbs. Sorry, what did you say, the 10th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, this date here, around June 1992 when Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10th June, yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 17th June.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 17th June. As I said, there were no Serbs. There were four Croats, and the rest were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And who were in the majority?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of this Crisis Staff were Muslims. They had an absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this conclusion we see that -- it says 150 CRD and 120 CRD. What is that? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that this staff dominated by the majority I described decided to designate the price in Croatian dinars because it was the only currency for which you could buy fuel at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm looking at this document. If I understand properly, on the 17th of June, 1992, in the Jablanica municipality we had a Muslim component. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour, but would you just clarify which component you meant, military or civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the civilian part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. They had an absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, they, with regard to the fuel prices, they are the ones establishing or using the Croatian dinar as the applicable currency; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understood properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, since we've had a bit of a pause, can I just ask since that issue has come up on majority, what I heard from the testimony was there were no Serbs. There were four Croats, and the rest were Muslim. I might wonder if counsel could assist us by how many were Muslims, other than just leaving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can ask that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- but certainly I can't let this go without noting this is a sort of question that should be coming up on cross-examination but since this is of interest to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how many Muslims were on the Crisis Staff at that time if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how many Croats again?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three -- four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00790. We see this is a decision, and if we look at the very last page, it's dated 10 August 1992, again signed by Mr. Nijaz Ivkovic. And here if we just look at -- look through the document we see mentioned, say in Article 6 or Article 7, we see references to the German mark. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course the German mark was not the official currency in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at the very last page, it says here: "All funds collected in this way shall be transferred to a special account of the Jablanica municipality Crisis Staff and shall be used to finance the general and collective needs of the population of Jablanica municipality and members of the armed forces in wartime conditions in the period of July/September 1992." Now, when it makes reference here to the -- to members of the armed forces, what is this document referring to as members of the armed forces? And we're speaking 10 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim armed forces are understood, not the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But at that point in time given your earlier testimony, was there still that agreement between 80 per cent and 20 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 00333. And here I want you to focus your attention to Article II, where it says: "In the entities referred to in item I of this order -- if the entities us referred to in item I of this order fail to meet their tax obligations in line with the current municipal regulations before the deadline set by the inspection team, which has been given powers to do the work of the financial police, in the public sector ..." And then if we go on to the Article III. Do you see that the BH armed forces are to be lending assistance in this process? Can you please help us without with this document? What exactly is happening, or what exactly is this order trying to do?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I can help. It's obvious that the tax levying decisions that were adopted were not being implemented. There is something unusual about this. The authority to levy taxes was something that the social income administration used to be in charge of before it was a municipal body, and now this is being passed along to some municipal secretariat for finance with the assistance of the armed forces and public security stations. Never before had taxes been collected in this way with the assistance of armed forces and public security stations so one thing is obvious that this is just not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Incidentally, I know I asked you yesterday, but perhaps you might help us out again focusing on this particular order. Did the -- the HVO in Jablanica, did they issue any such orders? In other words, to use the civilian HVO, to use members of the HVO military to go out and try to collect taxes in any particular area the HVO or the HZ HB was operating in Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01460. This is a decision on imposing war taxes on citizens. And just very briefly, can you tell us what currency now is being used as -- as a basis for tax collection?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this decision we are back to the German mark as the currency being used for taxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But if you look at, for instance, Article 3, it says: "It is hereby determined --" this is on the second paragraph of Article 3. "It is hereby determined that a tax of 20 per cent will be payable in BH dinars, and that the exchange rates shall be determined according to the market value." So based on this, was the BH dinar now circulating and, if so, what was its market value at the time, assuming it had one.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again the BH dinar was not around at the time. It wasn't just me. No one in Jablanica had ever set eyes on it. Therefore, it couldn't be used as a means of payment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was more of a psychological thing. That's the sort of value that it had in terms of its importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, what do you mean by that, very briefly, because it's kind of an elusive concept.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were talking about the fact that the BH dinar had come into existence, but it had not yet physically reached Jablanica. No one had so far set eyes on it. That was my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next chapter, and we're going to try to move a little quicker if we could. This deals with sort of the civilian authorities, and I first want to start off with document 1D 00785, dated 11 May 1992. This is a decision --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you just tell me what the name is for that chapter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I got ahead of myself. So move to the next -- the next chapter will be movement and mobilisation. I apologise. My documents got a little mixed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a question which -- a follow-up question which has nothing to do with the present document. I would like to know in your locality there was Banjica [as interpreted] at the time. Was there a bank agency, was there a branch? Was there a branch, a bank, or was there no branch of a bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I'm not quite certain about what you're trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question, in your locality, in your place Jablanica, in 1992 was there a bank or a branch of a bank? Was there any bank with a branch in this place, or was there no branch of a bank there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour, and I'll try to answer. There was a branch which was an outpost of the Sarajevo Privredna bank which had a local office in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So there was a branch in Jablanica. When people went to the bank to get some money or to deposit some money they deposited Croatian dinars or Deutschmarks? What currency were they using?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no one was depositing anything because the Yugoslav dinar had no value at all. As to the foreign currencies that you mentioned, those who had any, kept it back, because prior to the war there had been restrictions on how much one could take out of the bank. There needed to be a situation of urgency such as illness or something like that. One needed to show documents in order to collect a certain amount. People were not free to do as they saw fit with their foreign currencies even before the war. So no one even went to this bank. It was just another building just like the SDK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... more clearly. Witness, I also have a follow-up question. In which currency or money were the agents of the municipality were they paid, the officials of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the employees of the municipality were not being paid at all, and that included me. There were no salaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to follow up on the question that was asked by the President, going back to the first document in the previous chapter. That would be 1D 00973. This is the very first document that we started off today with. It says here "the PBS Sarajevo commercial bank." Do you see that? It's the very first document, right there. I think you have it right there. And if we go on and read the order it says that branches -- branch offices and post office to place all their material and technical equipment, resources, and money at the disposal of the Jablanica municipal crisis staff. Is that the same bank that you were just describing, or is this a different bank?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So for all intents and purposes, all the resources that this bank had by virtue of this order now were being used or at the disposal of the Crisis Staff. Is that how we're to understand this order?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order, yes, but I was there myself and I can tell you that the order never materialised. Those who had some cash in terms of dinars handed it over, and there was a foreign currency. They just hid it away, and there was nothing we could do about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to the next chapter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's first of all -- Witness, let's finish, but we have already devoted many hours to this. Each answer gives rise to a new question. I suppose that in Jablanica, whether it was Croats or Muslims, had members of their family working in Germany or in Italy or in Switzerland or in France, I don't know, and I suppose these people were sending them money, therefore -- to help them out. To help them out. Ol parent in Jablanica, elderly people, a son working in Frankfurt could send them a sum of money. And this money, was it going through the PBS bank in Jablanica? Was it going through that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. For as long as the PBS was still operating, these transactions did not go through the bank. One would simply physically bring the money back when returning from Germany or another country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next -- the next chapter dealing with movement and mobilisation. At least that's what we've titled it as. And I'm going to refer you to the first document. It's 1D 00781. 1D 00781. And we see that it's dated 10 April, 1992, signed by President Sefer Hamdo. Do you have that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And here it says that: "All citizens of Jablanica municipality are hereby advised not to move out of the municipality since the Presidency believes that there is no need for such actions as yet." Then it talks about -- I'll skip number 2. And in number 3 it says: "The municipal Presidency hereby forbids all citizens capable of working, and particularly persons eligible for military service, to leave the municipality." Can you please explain this to us? What is going on?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is more by way of information or announcement. It's a proclamation. It's not an order. Despite this proclamation people had already begun to move out because of what was happening in the broader Jablanica area. This proclamation was meant to be a pre-emptive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00782. We see a decision to set up check-points at the exits of Jablanica municipality. And then we can see that it's from Jablanica to Mostar, Konjic, and Prozor, and it talks about to improve traffic, security control, and to prevent theft. And I asked you this question yesterday: Who was implementing this particular decision? Who were manning, in other words, the check-points?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was being implemented by the reserve forces of the public security station. The reservists from the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, that was back in April 1992. Did that continue after April 1992 and into 1993, or did that situation change? In other words, were check-points at any given time manned by others?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the end of 1992, the situation changed significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. When that situation changed who was actually at those check-points?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was no longer just the police reserve. They were now joined by soldiers, soldiers from elsewhere who just happened to be in Jablanica as refugees. People from Foca, east Bosnia, Rogatica, Rudo, and so on and so forth. They put on uniforms and they started manning those check-points, which caused a great deal of concern among the locals because there were now people from other areas holding the check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, who was -- who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right if we look at the next document, 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, just not to remain in an error, it reads in the English text "partial roadblocks." Could you explain in what sense partial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, Your Honour. The road was not fully blocked. In Jablanica there was a Granit factory and sometimes these blocks weigh 12 tonnes or more. It was possible for us to simply drag two of those huge granite blocks along and simply half the road in terms of bread as it were. The road was not completely blocked. It was just narrowed as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document 1D 01447, just very briefly. This is a decision where it says: "The departure of vehicles abroad is hereby suspended..." and there was an exception. Why was this decision passed, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. The decision was passed on account of the fact that some vehicles by this time, and they're talking here about cars, company-owned cars, had left and went abroad by this time, and no one returned, not the persons driving those vehicles, not the vehicles themselves. So this was meant to be a pre-emptive thing and the reason it was passed is because some people had left already and did not seem to be returning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And they weren't returning the vehicles as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes. I've never seen a vehicle returned without the driver, have I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. 1D 01448. 17 April 1992. This is a decision. Here we see: "Citizens from 18 to 60 years of age fit for work are hereby banned from going abroad." What is this about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the ban imposed on military conscripts. They are being banned from going abroad. Age group 18 to 60. The only exception being medical treatment that was urgent and a number of other such exceptional is conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, what if somebody needed to go abroad because they fit with one of these exceptions? Did they need to get permission? Was there some sort of a permit, and, if so, who would issue that permit?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a permit would be issued, and this was something that was issued by the secretariat for All People's Defence, which was a municipal body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00960. Here's another order. This is April 28. "All Jablanica citizens from 18 to 60 ... who are subject to work obligation but left this municipality are hereby ordered to return within five days." Can you explain what this order was all about, even though it's somewhat self-evident?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Again we're talking about military conscripts. Despite all of these bans some managed to leave or were outside the municipal area when the ban came into force. Therefore, this is meant to be an order for them to return within five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But here it says: "All Jablanica citizens ... that are subject to work obligation." My question is would this include women as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this decision that would seem to be the case, because women, too, can be subject to work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00980. This is 14 May 1992, and this talks about immediately carrying out a general mobilisation, and it specifies Doljani local commune. Do you know why this was targeted to this particular location?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that the accused are not getting a translation -- or no one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just hearing my own --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Looking at this document 1D 00980, can you please tell us why there was an order for the immediate mobilisation to Doljani local commune? Why this commune, and not, let's say, other areas, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. The Jablanica Crisis Staff adopted this order because a day or two before, a military plane of the JNA had bombed the area around the villages specified. Therefore an order like this had to be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're gonna skip one document in order to save time. In fact, we can skip the next document as well, so we'll skip what's in your binder as 1D 00987 and 988, and let's just go straight to 1D 01455. This was 21 July 1992. Again, this is a general -- a decision on general mobilisation and again we see Doljani, Sovici, and Slatina. Can you please explain to us what is happening at this particular point in time, and why is this targeted to these particular areas?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly the same thing as the one before. This is about JNA military planes bombing this entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00343. This is 10 November now, 1992. Here we have an order which essentially says that all military fit persons between 18 and 55 that are on the territory of the Jablanica municipality, they're being ordered to return to their permanent place of residence by 20 November 1992. So here it looks like certain persons who are military fit are being asked to evacuate the Jablanica municipality and return to where they came from. Can you please explain what is happening? Are they being deported? Are they being forced out? What is going on?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not being forced out. They left at an earlier date of their own free will, but now the municipal Presidency is asking them back, telling them to get in touch with the BH armed forces Main Staff upon their return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I want to make sure that you understand me. Are they now to be mobilised in Jablanica municipality to fight for Jablanica, are they to return to where they came from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to follow from this that they should be returned to their place of permanent residence, which means the area that they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what if the area where they came from is -- is unsafe because there maybe military activity going on?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Jablanica's case this is precisely how it was like. All those from Eastern Bosnia who happened to be in or around Jablanica who were unable to return to their earlier places of residence, they were unable to return to east Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just ask one question. Why didn't the Jablanica municipality mobilise these military-aged men to have them fight for Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them had been mobilised by this time as needed. This is about further mobilisation, about further bringing up manpower levels in terms of mobilised persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Where are they supposed to be mobilised? I guess that's what I'm trying to -- if you could please look at Article I. Who is going to be mobilising them if it's not Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, forgive for interrupting, but I have the impression that we may have fallen back into asking the witness to simply read and talk about what he sees on the face of the document as opposed to what personal knowledge he can actually add to it. All of us in the courtroom can read the document. I mean, unless the witness has personal knowledge and can add something to it other than telling us what the document says and Mr. Karnavas now just points him to a particular part of the document and says, "Is that what it says," all we're doing is reading the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll lay a foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that point in time, sir, were you still in the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you in and around Jablanica at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please describe to us how many refugees were in Jablanica, particularly men of military age, between the ages of 18 to 55, if you know, from your personal observations being in Jablanica at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that. I was in the War Presidency until the 29th October. Until then we received daily reports from the headquarters for admission of refugees, and I had information until the month of October that the number of these refugees exceeded the local population of Jablanica, which was 12.600, according to the census. According to the estimate of the headquarters for admission of refugees the refugees at that time numbered over 15.000, and among them there were 5 to 7.000 military-age men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, 1D 01007. Here's an order that all refugees liable for military service from the area of Eastern Bosnia who are currently in the territory of Jablanica municipality, they're being asked to return to those areas. If you know, at that point this time, this is 11 April 1993, what is happening in Eastern Bosnia, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Eastern Bosnia this time and for a year before, there was a war going on. The Serb forces attacked Eastern Bosnia about a year before this date, and the war was going on. This order simply could not be enforced, nor could anyone go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you would go to 1D 00349. This is an order by Dr. Cibo, dated 25 April 1993. And here we see he's calling for immediate mobilisation, and we see the ages of 15 to 65. Now, from your experiences, is the age 15, is that unusual or was that common at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know this is unusual, because only those who are of age can be mobilised, that means over 18. This, however, indicates 15 to 65, and this decision is contrary to what we had read before. The previous document said they should leave Jablanica, and this one says once they are in Jablanica already they should be mobilised into the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll go on to the next chapter, and this deals with civilian authorities. And the first document is 1D 00785. Just very quickly. This is 11 May 1992, and we see that this is a decision on your -- you being elected to the Executive Committee or chairman of the Executive Committee of Jablanica municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And by virtue of this position now you are a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next -- next one is 1D 01456. Here this is 21 July 1992, and here we see that the Crisis Staff is being renamed to the War Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I know we touched upon it yesterday a little bit, but did the composition of the War Presidency change in any way? In other words, were new members added and, if so, where would they have come from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the composition changed when I came, because I replaced a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I'm not speaking as far as ethnicities. What I'm saying is did they -- did additional members come on board the War Presidency, say, from other institutions? Okay. So all --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- in other words?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 03038, that's the next document. And this is dated 29 October 1992, and by this decision we see that you are being relieved as president of the Executive Board of Jablanica municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was actually replaced and sent to temporary work at the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And this document, where did this come from? Had you seen this document before, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received it in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did you give this document to the Defence, to us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, can we get the number again, it wasn't in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in this document it says that you are being temporarily sent to work in the public security station. Had you ever -- had you had any training in public security matters?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when it says temporarily, what does that mean, and how was it that you were sent there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thing was temporary because the Presidency was aware that the procedure of regulating one's legal and employment status in the police had to be determined in Sarajevo, and it was physically impossible to reach Sarajevo, and they were perfectly aware that I could not go there and get the idea of an authorised police officer, and that's why they wrote temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right 1D 00324. This is 29 October 1992, and here is a decision to elect the chairman and members of the Executive Committee, and now we see that it's Ivan Rogic who is being elected chairman of the Executive Committee of Jablanica municipality. I take it this is the individual that replaced you. Is that correct? And he's a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And all the other members that we can see that were being elected, they are Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to the next document, 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One technical matter, Mr. Karnavas. Document 1D 03038, is it part of the 65 ter list or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- this is a document that we received from the gentleman when he came. We sent it to everyone. And the reason that I mentioned where we got -- I wanted the gentleman to confirm that he gave this document to us was to lay the foundation as to how it came into our possession. We received this when the gentleman arrived. We had it translated, and we circulated it to everyone. And we will be adding it to the 65 ter list. But this was just to confirm that he was -- the date of his departure from the -- as the president of the Executive Board. Can I continue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 00338. This is now 7 -- 2nd November 1992, and this is a decision on setting up a commission to resolve incidents occurring in the Jablanica municipality, and we see that the very first person as president of the commission is Matan Zaric. He's obviously a Croat; correct? And as I --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, and I could be wrong, he was also the president of the HDZ in Jablanica municipality, or do I have it wrong?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the vice-president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. My apologies. And just very briefly, why is it necessary to set up this commission? What is happening around 2nd November 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was still a member of the War Presidency, we received reports from the public security station on the high incidence of violation of law and order, robbery and aggravated robbery and looting, so the War Presidency was trying to do something. It formed this working group with the idea that they would be actually going out into the field and talking to people, but as far as I know it didn't come to much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01461. Now, this is dated 12 January 1993, and if we look -- this is a statement in the media, BH radio and TV. And if we look at the very last paragraph, it says: "The Jablanica War Presidency is appealing to the leadership of SDA and the HDZ to continue their efforts on finding solutions for a harmonious and peaceful life of all citizens of Jablanica municipality." Let's start there. At this point in time -- and this is 12 January 1993, and I underscore this for the Trial Chamber's attention. At this point in time, what are the relations between SDA and HDZ, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of either, and at that time I was not a member of the War Presidency either. I know of this communique as a regular citizen because I was following the news. There had been sparks between the SDA and the HDZ because of incidents at Christmas, the bombing of the church, the throwing of grenades outside the HDZ staff, or HVO staff, attacks, assaults made by one refugee from Foca and a number of other incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that there was an attack or a bombing on the HVO staff. Now, are we talking about military or are we talking the civilian premises?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the office for the accommodation of the military members of the HVO. It was an office in an office building, and this grenade was thrown outside the office of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you know about what time, what period this would have been?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened almost the same day as the attack on the church. Sometime before Christmas. That is, before the 25th December a grenade was thrown outside the Catholic church, and perhaps just a day later or a day before a grenade was thrown at the HVO office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did the HVO office, incidentally, did it have a flag? Is it flying the colours of the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, is that the flag of the republic -- is that the flag of the Republic of Croatia, or is that the flag of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because there are differences. Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the flag of the Republic of Croatia. It was the flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. How long had that flag been flying in relation to the bombing incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back to this -- this statement very briefly because there may be some questions from the Bench, we see from the very first paragraph "BH radio and TV." Could you please tell us at that point in time, and now we're speaking 12 January 1993, was there radio and television reception in Jablanica municipality and, if so, where was it coming from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: BH TV could be received. It was transmitted through these repeaters. What quality it was, I don't know, but it was not the only one. Other stations from Bosnia and Herzegovina could be received too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what about Jablanica? Did Jablanica have a local TV programme?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jablanica had local cable television broadcasting its own programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I see that on line 11 it says other stations. Are we talking about other radio stations or other television stations? Which of the two? Not in the document. I just see it in the transcript here that you're -- sir. Mr. Zelenika, it's not in the document. We can see what was being translated. How many television stations, channels, I should say, were you able to have at that point in time in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Jablanica, in addition to the BH television programme, we were able to watch the Croatian radio television as well. However, there was some technical interference later and we were no longer able to watch Croatian TV, but I cannot confirm at this moment whether we could watch Croatian TV in -- on this date in 1993, but I would say not. But in 1992 and in 1991, we were certainly able to watch Croatian TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how many -- how many radio stations were you able to -- or channels were you able to pick up on? Radio.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depended on your receiver.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it was able to catch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1-01464. The next document 1D 01464. Here we have a decision and we see Mirsad Klepo is now being elected to the executive committee. And we take it he is replacing Mr. Rogic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this individual is a Muslim, is he not?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So as I understand it he's not SDA, he's SDP, SDP.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that point in time, now with the replacement of the only Croat on the Executive Committee, at least what we saw earlier, how many Croats are now on the Executive Committee of Jablanica municipality? And we're speaking of 4 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single Croat remained on the Executive Board of Jablanica at the time we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 02753. This is a decision on release from duty and election of presidents and members of the War Presidency of the Municipal Assembly, and we can see from Article I, it makes reference to Jablanica and Konjic. And I want to direct your attention and everyone else's attention to Roman numeral XV, XVI and XVII. Now, sir we see that Dr. Cibo is now becoming the president of Jablanica and Konjic municipalities, and then it further says -- they have the listing of all those people who have been elected, and then it says that on 7 -- on 17: "For the purposes of providing ethnic representation in War presidencies of municipal assemblies, a war Presidency shall propose electing the necessary number of Presidency members from among the Serbs and the Croats." And this is signed by Alija Izetbegovic. Now, to your understanding having worked in government, having been in the -- the president of the Executive Council twice, once in the 1980s and again prior to -- in 1992, can you please tell us whether this decision by President Izetbegovic is lawful and constitutional?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision by Mr. Izetbegovic is unconstitutional, unlawful, and actually constitutes both the legal and political precedent concerning appointments to local bodies of authority and government. This decision is contrary to all the laws that applied in our state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll go on to the next document, 1D 02756. And now here we have an order by Sefer Halilovic, and we see that under 1, Safet Cibo is being appointed to a particular position. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us -- this is now 20 March 1993. Can you please explain to us what is happening in this particular order? And again I want you to reflect back to your experience and knowledge at the time having been in and around Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to explain this order. The document we viewed before we said was unconstitutional and unlawful. We're now a legally elected president an ethnic Muslim was replaced by a man from Sarajevo. But that's not all. This now imposed president from Sarajevo gets by virtue of this order -- rather, gives powers to the 4th Corps to command the military units of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And he actually did exercise that command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that you spoke too fast. I'm going to ask you to please go back and -- and give us that explanation. My time is limited, so it's better to just speak clearly, slowly, so we can get it all.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. When I speak at length, I speak fast, but I'll try. The document that we viewed a moment ago when we said that our legally elected president of the municipality in Jablanica was unlawfully replaced, Mr. Nijaz Ivkovic, an ethnic Muslim, and a man from Sarajevo was imposed on us, Dr. Safet Cibo. But that was not enough. This new unlawfully imposed president, by virtue of this order we are seeing now, is vested with powers to issue orders and commands to the 4th Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02757. This is 20 March 1993, and we see that at a meeting of the central office and parts of the Executive Committee of the SDA: "1. Dr. Safet Cibo is hereby co-opted to the -- to Herzegovina Regional Board as a full member." And then if we go to the very last part of this document it says: "This decision was also issued in order to improve the work of the party in Herzegovina." Can you please explain to us what is happening with this particular decision that's being made? Dr. Cibo being co-opted into the Herzegovina Regional Board.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a textbook example of a coincidence. The document we've just seen is also dated 27th March, and this one is dated 20th March. Since Dr. Cibo, permanently residing in Sarajevo, could not be elected in regular -- regular elections to the Regional Board of the SDA to Herzegovina, he is co-opted to the Regional Board of the SDA in Herzegovina, as they put it, to improve the work of the party in Herzegovina on the position to which he was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we're talking about -- this is 20th of March; correct? The document.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, along with this document there's a handwritten note, and could you please tell us what this note is about? What does it say? Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Go for it.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were not from Jablanica, I wouldn't be able to help you, but since I hail from Jablanica, it's fine. This is handwritten. It says: "Zijo," meaning Zijad Demirovic, at that time president of the Regional Board of the SDA Mostar, and it says: "Zijo, this morning Almisa confirmed to me that the appointment of Dr. Cibo is all right. Since Avdo will be going up there tomorrow, let him get information on that as well." Then we see the Muslim greeting, Mahusuz Selam, and this is the signature.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear whose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Jablanica. Cibo is therefore coming to Jablanica, because as we saw from the previous document, he was politically co-opted. We don't see from this directly that he was coming from Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You need to slow down because again we're spending more of my time trying to correct the translation here. Tell us again what is happening in this note, and I'm going to ask you to kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I read this handwritten note rather slowly, but this second part is when I said that the purpose is to express satisfaction that Dr. Cibo was co-opted to the Regional Board of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well that will be after the break. It's now 10.30. We are going to break for 20 minutes. You still have one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Start again, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we start, I need to bring to the Court's attention an error on our part. There were three documents that were given to us by the witness, 1D 03038, 1D 03040, and 1D 03041. 39 -- 3039 and 3040, and under the guidelines we were supposed to seek permission to add to the 65 ter before using them with the witness, and this was an oversight. I take full responsibility for that, and I just -- it was brought to my attention. So I just want to make sure that we're clear on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Going back to the last document, sir, where you read out from that handwritten note, if you could please tell us who signed it. Do you recognise the signature on the document, on that little note?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Muhamed Murvat, a teacher from Jablanica and a member of the municipal at the time. Muhamed Murvat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document 1D 02777, and -- do you have it, is, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And this appears to be dated March 25, 1993. If we look at the bottom, it's president of the War Presidency, and this would be of Konjic. Do you recognise the gentleman's name? Okay. And who --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- is that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Rusmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does he have a last name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hadzihusejnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would appear that here the president of the Konjic municipality is objecting in a manner in which Dr. Cibo replaced him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you know anything about how -- what, if anything, I should say, this gentleman did upon receiving this notification that he was being relieved? Did he accept it passively, or did he do anything?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from writing this letter, he took other steps too. He physically refused to leave the office of the president of the War Presidency in Konjic. When he took that decision, he was physically carried away. He had to be physically removed. He was arrested by the police and the army in Konjic, and they physically removed him from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02758. This is dated 27 April 1993. Now, you indicated earlier the significance between -- the significance of Dr. Cibo being appointed by Halilovic to give -- to a position within the 4th Corps. If we look at this particular document, can you please explain to us what is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. This is an illustration of how Mr. Cibo, based on the schedule or assignment, the document that we looked at a while ago, the 4th Corps. So based on that he's issuing a specific order to the Muslim units to take two positions. One is Ljubina. It reads "Ljubina must fall tonight. Ljubina is an elevation above Konjic known as a very important communications centre belonging to the former JNA previously. There was a lot of equipment there. And now this position was held by the HVO. Therefore, Ljubina must fall. And then the next thing, Boksevica must fall as soon as possible. Boksevica is a mountain in both Konjic and Jablanica municipality. It too was being handled at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Interpreters note] Could all microphones be switched off while the witness is speaking, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when we look at the one Ljubina must fall tonight, that's a borrowed line, isn't it, from Tito? Using Tito's line "Prozor must fall tonight;" right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the fourth enemy offensive, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we go to the next document 1D 01013. This is dated 29 April 1993. We have seen earlier the appointment of Dr. Cibo, and we have seen in paragraph, I believe it was, Roman numeral XVII where it indicated that other nationals should be included. So in looking -- keeping that in mind, let's look at this document, and I want to focus your attention to number 5 and number 6. We have a Serb and a Croat. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then of course if we look at number 12, he see the chairman of HDZ and -- okay. Now, to your knowledge were these individuals ever serving on -- as members of the War Presidency of the Jablanica municipality? Did they ever serve?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Jablanica at the time. I know both these persons. As a matter of fact, I asked them the question at the time. Neither of them were ever even aware of the fact that anybody had put their names on this list. That's one thing. And the other is these two persons are not from Jablanica at all. Cedomir Tipuric is from Konjic but by matter of coincidence he was in Jablanica staying with his girlfriend at the time the war broke out. Milan Manigoda is an engineer hails from Jablanica originally, but 15 years before the war, he had been living in Mostar and it was by pure coincidence that he ended up in Jablanica at this time. This is the equivalent of actually having a bus pass through Jablanica and then you simply order the bus to pull over, you pick out a couple of people who are aboard that bus and you appoint them members of the Presidency. The long and the short of it, they were not involved in the work of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if we look at this paper, on its face it would give the appearance at least that now we have a multi-ethnic War Presidency in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as I have to comment on this, this is the impression that someone might get who is just reading this without actually knowing what was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at the next document 1D 01308. Here we have a decision dated 31 July 1993, and of course it's signed by none other than Alija Izetbegovic, and it would appear as we look under Roman numeral II, we see again under number 5, Milan Manigoda, and number 6, Mr. Tipuric. And of course number 12, we see the president of the Deputies' Club of HDZ. Now, this is several months after the previous document. Do you know whether the situation changed on 31 July 1993, or is this decision another charade being perpetrated by Alija Izetbegovic and others?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, pursuant to this proposal that had arrived from Mr. Cibo in Jablanica, merely confirmed what it says about Mr. Manigoda, Mr. Tipuric, the HDZ president, although a while ago as I was commenting on that document, I didn't say that, but I'm about to say it now. There were no representatives of the HDZ in this Presidency simply because he was physically not present when the meetings of the Presidency were held, nor was he able to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we're going to look at the next documents more or less together, and that's 1D 01070, and 1D 01063. They're both dated 14th June 1993, both signed by Dr. Cibo. If we look at the first one 1D 01070, under paragraph Roman numeral I, paragraph -- or item number 2 it says: "It is necessary to gather the leaders and members of the HDZ in Jablanica in order to review and resolve the problems of the Croatian citizens so that they may feel like the other local peoples." And of course if you look at the decision under Roman numeral I, it says in order to increase overall mobility and fight for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina more completely and effectively we are hereby establishing the united front in the struggle for the sovereign and indivisible Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as recognised by the world. Now, sir, where it says on the first document, 1D 01070, "to gather the leaders," were you -- did you ever participate in any meetings concerning these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please describe to us how is it that you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please describe to us how is it you were at this meeting or meetings and what, if anything, occurred?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at a meeting organised by Mr. Cibo on the 12th of June. He called a meeting. He had previously described the meeting as a meeting between the Muslim intellectuals and successful businessmen including representatives of the local Serbs and Croats. This included also UNPROFOR representatives, ICRC people, and UNHCR. From the ranks of the Muslims there were some people who came who he believed to be intellectuals, and there were a couple of businessmen who were owners of private enterprises in the area. The Serbs were represented by Mr. Gojko Jelacic, a Serbs from Jablanica. On behalf of the Croats there were the parish priest Alojlije Bosnjak, Mr. Jure Juric, the local butcher from Jablanica, a Croat, and I was there too. Mr. Cibo made a lengthy introduction that took nearly 45 minutes to complete. He tried to explain something, and it was down to this: It is normal for a wall to be white. If someone were to draw a single black dot on that wall, we'd all start staring at it wondering what is this black dot? So he goes, "This black spot in this white world, it's the HVO, and it needs to be wiped out." And then after that he asked for all those present, by a show of hands, to lend their support to this proposal that he made to organise a united front to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was adamant that a vote should be taken, but I refused to be involved, and I refused to watch what all the others were doing. So I ended up saying, "Mr. Chairman, let me take this opportunity to tell you about the many problems faced by the Croats following the clashes between the BH army and the HVO, and I mean the Croats who just happen to be in this area under the control of the BH army." And then I said, they're being -- they're being ousted from their flats. They are being robbed and looted." And the first thing I asked is, "When will you finally release those of our civilians who are in the Museum?" And they were about 30 of those by this time. Following my contribution he said as follows: "I now close the meeting, and I call upon all Croats tomorrow at 10.00," I'm talking about the 13th of June, "to come to this conference room." The next day -- did I say -- I said the 13th of June, yes. The 13th of June at 10.00. The next day at 10.00 we were all there. I think about 74 of us assembled as a matter of fact. And then we provided him with a detailed blow by blow account of everything. I myself spoke for about seven to ten minutes. He took an hour and a half to explain whatever he had to explain in relation to what I had said. When he came to the captured Croats, he said there were proceedings under way to check whether anyone had committed any crimes. As long as that was not the case, everyone would be issued with a certificate to the effect that they were totally innocent, and they would be free to move about, and they would get the certificate to avoid someone arresting them in the street. Perhaps I was a bit gullible here myself because that never materialised. That never materialised. Talking about that museum in which they were being kept, several hundred Croats later arrived at that museum who were also captured. This museum was a camp. It remained like that until the end of 1993, and there were over 600 Croat prisoners that at various points in time were held there. The greatest number of civilians. As for these two documents, this conclusion and the next one, when I read these I had the feeling that it was my speech, my contributions at these two meetings that had been the inspiration behind these two documents. That's one thing. But other thing is that had I not attended that meeting, had I not say a thing, these conclusions -- neither one of these conclusions would ever have materialised. So there you have it. That's my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Couple of points. One, this is June 14 we have these conclusions. You indicated the meeting took place on the 12th and the 13th. Yesterday you told us -- yesterday you told us that you were essentially doing slave labour as a result of your condition and the work that they were actually forcing you to do.
