Were you doing this sort of labour during this period when Dr. Cibo summoned you to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, before the witness answers I'm going to object to the characterisation of slave labour. I don't think that was the way it was used -- described yesterday. I think the witness said being mobilised into a civilian work detail to him was forced labour. I don't remember anything being said about slave labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll leave the record to whatever the gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I don't know about slave labour. I know he had to unload trucks. Is unloading trucks slave labour? I don't know. Would you please reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was the gentleman's characterisation, but I'll reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You told us that you had a medical condition; correct? You need to answer the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You told us that you had documentation to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You told us that -- that this was well known and would have been documented already; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And those documents would have been in the possession of the Territorial Defence office.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You also told us that you -- they refused to provide to allow -- to conduct a medical examination.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I think liberty is -- with all due respect to Mr. Karnavas, I think he's taking liberties with the record. I don't think that's the way it was characterised it. I don't know why we're going back to these points. I do agree this testimony -- general testimony was given yesterday and the only reason I see it appears that Mr. Karnavas is going back to put his particular spin on the evidence. I don't remember anything about anyone refusing to conducting a medical examination or whether who had the papers or didn't. So I don't have any -- if he wants to recover the same ground by not -- excuse me -- by non-leading questions and repeat the same answers as yesterday that's one thing, but I think we're just spinning the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the record should reflect first and foremost this objection was prompted not by his memory but by his colleague, and the record, the record is rather very clear. Mr. Scott seems to just simply wish to object for the sake of objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, did you ask for a medical examination and, if so, was one provided to you in order to demonstrate that you indeed had a physical disability and could not perform the labour which you were being asked to perform?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sent for treatment, but when I was received by a doctor, there was no examination. He refused to examine me, and he refused to even look at the -- the very comprehensive documentation that I had brought along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At this point in time when you were summoned by Dr. Cibo, were you working? Were you doing that sort of work that you were forced to do?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two days. The 12th and the 13th of June when I was off to that meeting at Dr. Cibo's, I did not perform forced labour. But this was far worse than slave labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But my point is prior to these -- prior to these meetings were you working in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it possible that Dr. Cibo didn't know what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that at one point you raised the issue of Croats being in the museum and as to when they would be released. Are we speaking about the same museum that you were ultimately taken to and kept?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how far would that museum have been from Dr. Cibo's office?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 600 and 700 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did you ever try to -- to get out of the museum? Did you ever make any applications that would bring you to someone's attention, say, within the civilian government?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I never had an opportunity. Not just me, none of those captured had any opportunity to get in touch and talk to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm not speaking whether you spoke to them directly, but did there ever come a time because of your mother's illness that you made an attempt for someone to intervene on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried through my relatives for them to address whoever was responsible for my provisional release, a short-term one from the camp, but they then informed me that the reply from the person responsible was negative, that I would not be allowed to go to hospital to visit my mother. So I ended up not going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who is the person that was responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time it was Mr. Dzelmo Zenaid. He was some sort of an inspector in the local public security station. He was in charge of setting the pace in terms of living conditions inside the museum, in terms of when prisoners could receive visits, in terms of deciding whether a prisoner would be allowed to leave the museum in order to go see a doctor. He was the person who set the pace in terms of what went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did you ever try to contact any of your former colleagues from the War Presidency through an intermediary to see if they could intervene on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never tried. Although when I lift the camp, I asked my father if anyone had ever asked about me, because my father would see all these people on a daily basis. Jablanica was a small town, and we all knew each other. But then my father said that no one ever asked any questions about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it possible that Dr. Cibo didn't know that you were in the basement of the museum?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Cibo came to the museum many times. He knew very well who was in there. True, I couldn't see him myself because I was in the basement, and he would go up to the first floor normally. And I believe at least 500 other prisoners saw him on a number of different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very quickly, if we go to the next document, 1D 00774. And just very quickly, this is August 29, 1993. We see this decision by Dr. Cibo, and again we see the two names that we mentioned earlier under number 9 and number 10. We don't see anybody as a representative of HDZ. And I take it as of August 29, 1993, these two individuals, Tipuric and Milan Manigodic, they were not members?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't. They'd fled Jablanica by this time. They paid someone to help them get away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We go on to the next document, 1D 01027. This is dated 29 August 1993. This is on the appointment of the members and secretaries of the Jablanica municipal Executive Committee, and we look at those names. Do you see among those names any Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it they're all Muslim. There are no Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next document 1D 01500. And this is to set up a municipal commission for gathering facts and information about war crimes. 2 September 1993. We look at under Roman numeral II. We see five -- five names. Are any members of this municipal commission Croat?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none. No Croat, no Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We look at the next decision, 1D 01031. This is 17 September 1993. This is to replace the director of the Jablanica adult education centre, and we see that under Roman numeral I, Jozefina Dzalto is being replaced by Mirzo Pelic. Is Jozefina Dzalto a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jozefina Dzalto is an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what Mirzo Pelic, her replacement? She's being replaced by him. What is he?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirzo Pelic is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We go to the next document 1D 01042. This is January 10, 1994, and this is a decision appointing an election, an appointment committee, and this is for the Jablanica municipality. We see seven names there. Of the seven names, could you please tell us how many Muslim and how many Croats are there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All are Muslim here. There are no Croats, no Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 01043. This is a decision on appointing members of the secretaries of the executive committee of Jablanica. We're in 1994. This is dated 10 January 1994. And can you confirm to us the ethnic make-up of the Executive Committee of Jablanica municipality at this point in time? How many Croat, how many Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a mono-ethnic group. Everybody is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then finally 1D 00791. Again 10 January 1994. This is on the formation of the Presidency of the Jablanica Municipal Assembly. And we see the very first name Ivkovic. We've seen him before; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivkovic returns again to the position of president of the municipality from which he was recalled in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then under number 7 we also see Mirsad Klepo. He had been in that position at one point in time having, I believe, Rogic -- he had replaced Rogic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of the nine names here, can you please tell us what the ethnic are -- is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here again we see a mono-ethnic group. Everybody is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where is Dr. Cibo at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Cibo had performed the work for which he had come and returned to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to 1D 01009, and this chapter deals with mobilisation of resources. Just some vignettes for the Trial Chamber. This is 20 April 1993. This is under Cibo. And we see that all the chopped wood in the house of Mato Bilos is to be requisitioned. Now is Mato Bilos, is he a Muslim or is he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mato Bilos is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, 1D 01010. Here we're talking about flour and other foodstuffs to be expropriated from the Croatian Defence counsel shop and warehouse in Jablanica for the needs of the defence of the Jablanica municipality. Now, what do you know about this particular warehouse and who owned it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This warehouse was set up by the HVO of Jablanica municipality. There was a grocery there, and it was seized, confiscated for the needs of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether this was also happening to Muslims? Was Cibo targeting Muslims and Serbs as well, assuming there were any Serbs at the time there. But my -- my particular interest is in Muslims. Were they being -- were their foodstuffs being taken away, their chopped wood?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. These measures were taken only against Croats and Serbs in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at 1D 01011. This is 22 April 1993. And here it says: "Rationed goods requisitioned pursuant to the order of this War Presidency." And it gives a number of 16 April 1993. It may be used exclusively for the requirement of members of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina army, citizens and members of platoons. Can you please tell us whether the use of these requisitioned goods were also being given to the HVO military, or was this strictly for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, absolutely not, because at that time there was no HVO in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Next document, 1D 01012. It says here by this order "Because of the newly arisen war situation immediately start seizing all materials and goods necessary for the army of the republic of BH from state-owned and private companies..." Now, my question is this particular order, to your understanding, was it applied to everyone across the board, or were some members of the community excluded, or some companies?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about companies, whether anything was seized from them, but as for physical persons, this granted the legal right to members of the army and the police, and they exercised this right, to go from garage to garage, office building to office building, business to business breaking in the door and taking whatever they wanted to take. If anybody wanted to -- a receipt, they gave it. I had to unlock my door as well. I gave them my boat and some timber. They asked me if I wanted a receipt. I said no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What were they planning on doing with the boat in the middle of this chaos in war? Were boats being used for military purposes? I understand that there is the Neretva. It has pretty good fishing, but ...

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 01483. This is 18 May 1993, and here we can see that what is being requisitioned is the stock of medicine from the pharmacy of the Jablanica branch of the Caritas Croatian Catholic charity organisation, and now it's being handed to the Jablanica town pharmacy for better use. Do you know what was the problem with the Caritas pharmacy that Dr. Cibo, now a medical doctor, was confiscating the medicine supposedly to put it to better use?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose this was the last order. I believe that after this there was nothing more to take away from Croats. In Jablanica in 1991, a Croat Christian charity was organised which had some medication and medical supplies that a doctor and a nurse provided, handed out to all the citizens without regard to ethnicity, and the other part was humanitarian aid, mainly food. All that was stored in one shop, and in the parish office. The shop I just mentioned, now these medical supplies, the pharmacy owned by HKDD, is -- are now also seized, and this charity is closed down, this humanitarian organisation that served all citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I just want to make sure I understand correctly. The Caritas pharmacy, was it selling the medicine for profit? Was it selling it at base price, or giving it away for free to all those who actually needed it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The medicines were given free of charge to those who needed them under the supervision of one doctor and one woman pharmacist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was it strictly for -- for Croats, or could other citizens in Jablanica go there, that is, non-Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was for all the inhabitants of Jablanica. At that time the Muslims were in the majority, so there's reason to believe that they benefitted from a large part of this aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now we're going to go to the next chapter which deals with camps. The first document goes back to an earlier discussion. That's 1D 01492. This is sort of a housekeeping matter. It's dated 15 June 1993. This is an order and it says: "The Jablanica war hospital is hereby ordered to review all sick leaves of military conscripts through a military medical board." And my question to you, sir, is when I asked you earlier if you had been given the opportunity to be examined, physically examined, when you were asked to report for work obligation, would it have been at this particular hospital, the Jablanica war hospital, or was it some place else?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the place. I went to the Jablanica hospital and was

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: All right. And very briefly, we'll just go through some documents here. 1D 01847. This is 16 May 1993. This is a list of Croats imprisoned in a museum in Jablanica, and do you see those names, sir, and do you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: All right. The next document is 1D 01859. This is dated 16 May 1993. List of civilians of the Croatian ethnicity detained and kept in a blockade in Jablanica. And if you could look at -- if you could assist us here, and I'm going to focus your attention to numbers 207 and 208 on the list, which is the last page. Actually, it would be 207, 208, and 210. 207 it says Mirko Zelenika. That's you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: And 208 Marko Zelenika, that's your brother?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: And then Ivan and Ilka Zelenika, that's your father and mother?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We go on to the next document, 1D 01860. Here is another list, and if you could look at number 90. We see Marko Zelenika. That's your mother, is it not, number 90?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: And number 153, that would be -- that's you; correct? Mirko Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: And we go on to the next document which is 1D 0172. Here we don't see your name. This is of the 18th July 1993. Do you know -- do you know any of these individuals that are listed, and can you confirm whether these are -- this is a list of Croatian civilians and military conscripts from the Grabovica -- Donja Grabovica and the others that were captured and detained in Jablanica? Can you confirm that for us? Do you know? There are in total, I think --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that from this list I know several persons, and they are precisely from the locality you mentioned. That locality belongs to Mostar municipality. They had been captured there as civilians and brought to the museum camp in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A correction to the record, please. The document is not 1D 0172 as indicated but 1D 01712. I see you also had it. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Tomanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Okay. If we go on to the next document. 1D 00772. And perhaps we could park here for a little bit, and we can describe what is happening. This is dated 29 July 1993. This is a decision by Dr. Cibo, and I'll just read it out. I would ask you to please follow along or read it in the original. It says: "Except for members of the Croatian Defence Council, all persons from the Doljani local commune accommodated at present in Bitka Na Neretvi, the Battle of The Neretva museum in Jablanica may, provided they reach a mutual agreement, take temporary shelter in the homes of their relatives, friends or acquaintances in the free territory of Jablanica municipality." Can you please comment on this particular decision.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is simply impossible. This is nonsense. It's nonsense that the War Presidency could have made a decision like this. Only a day before, on the 28th of June, 1993, members of the BH army attacked the area of Doljani, and in that action on that day, they killed 39 Croats, among them a large number of civilians. Eighteen of them were seriously wounded, and all of them, 214 in total including 67 children under 15, and there were also several men, over 80 elderly women, all of them 214 of them were taken to the museum camp, and these 214 people stayed there for eight months. They were deliberately starved resulting in four deaths. At least two women were raped and all the others were victims of cruel and inhuman treatment by the camp personnel during eight months. This camp was registered by the ICRC, and it was visited by the ICRC several times. In all aspects it was like a Nazi camp, and the treatment was the same as in Nazi camps in World War II. That's how it was. And I was indignant to read that somebody was able, just a day after these people were captured and taken away from their homes to write a decision like this.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction the month was July, not June.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was still in the apartment of my parents, and I was still going to forced labour assignments, and I saw those people when they were brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas. Could you enlighten the Chamber about the relevance of this and why it is not tu quoque, because I must confess that I feel a bit lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, the issue of the individuals being kept in the museum has come up. On 8 November 2006, we had the testimony of Safet Idrizovic. You may recall, you may not. It's been a long time. He was questioned. He was shown a list. In fact, that's the next document, 6D 00035, and he at first claimed that he knew nothing about this. In fact, he states when he was asked quite pointedly, he says, I believe, "This wasn't part of the duties," meaning the military police, and the people who were in Doljani and who were brought from Doljani to the museum weren't detainees. They hadn't been in prison." Now, at some point you'll be sitting around with your colleagues to determine what are the facts, and of course this is testimony elicited by the Prosecution. Here we have confirmation that much of what Mr. Idrizovic is saying, and that would be my next two questions, is it goes to his credibility. And if the gentleman is confabulating, and I dare say I'll put it more bluntly, lying about this, then how can you possibly take the rest of his testimony without being somewhat circumspect. So that is the purpose. It goes to in part to impeach a witness from the Prosecution and this is a form of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a convincing and helpful answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Now, do you recall an incident that happened in your house when -- when these folks came and were put in the museum, do you recall an incident in your house with a little kid making certain remarks? And could you please describe to the Trial Chamber what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already earlier before this date pursuant to a decision of the War Presidency, I had to receive and accommodate a Muslim family from Rogatica counting nine members. When the army attack occurred and when the civilians were brought, I saw those people passing by on trucks, and later when I came into the apartment, a boy who could have been 10 or 11, and he resided at that time in my apartment, who had been to the museum and come back was talking to his mother, and he said, "Mum, I had been down there to target Ustashas," and the woman, I suppose, understood what it was all about and gestured to him to shut up. In Jablanica those women, children, and the elderly, those were the Ustashas that needed to be taken from Doljani to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Now, if I can look -- if I can have you look at 6D 00035. And this is a list compiled. It's a list of persons situated in the SRZ museum Jablanica, who were not members of the HVO. Let me ask you first, do you know what SRZ means?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to help me out here.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know, that's fine. Do you know the 6th Corps Military Police Battalion? Had you heard of them?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: If you look at the list of the names, do you know any of the names?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Are they from Jablanica, or are they from outside Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this list, as far as I can see, and I haven't seen this before, there are names and surnames of people brought from Doljani. I also see the name of my aunt from Jablanica. And indeed a number of people from Jablanica were driven out of their homes and taken to the museum, between 50 and 70 persons. And those people were never ever registered officially by anyone, because when the ICRC came, those people would be removed and hidden from the ICRC. So officially it turns out they had never been to the camp, because all the other inmates have a certificate from the -- certificate from the ICRC that they had been detained in that camp, and I am one of them.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, what is your -- what is your aunt's name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anica Rotim.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: And which one would be that?

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: And how do you know that the names are from Doljani? You say -- how did you -- how are you able to tell?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had two minutes to look at this list, I think I know over 80 per cent of these people. Anyone older than 30. Perhaps, I don't know, younger people. Because I was born in that locality. I have a weekend cottage there. I went there often before the war. I still go there and I know 80 per cent of those people who are still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just -- another rectification. I have heard and it has been recorded that you said, Witness, that your aunt was number 57. I wonder whether it is correct. Should you not go down two more? If you look at the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You need to put your glasses on, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. It's actually 59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Now, just one -- one point. Did you know an individual by the name of Safet Idrizovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: And how do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him because I lived for 35 years in Jablanica and so did he.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked there. Maybe we worked together --

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in certain periods.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: During this particular period that we're speaking of, did you know what, if anything, Mr. Idrizovic was doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time he was chief of the staff of the armed forces of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Do you think it's possible given his position that he would not have known what was happening or who was being kept at the museum? Is that plausible?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I object to speculation unless the witness has some personal -- some foundation of personal knowledge. Is it possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Idrizovic at or around the museum when you were being kept there, or even prior to that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: And incidentally, his offices, do you know how far they would have been at the time, if now know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the museum you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: From the museum, right.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have certainly taken more than four hours now, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I have about five minutes left, Your Honour, that's about it, if I could.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: If I go on to the next document 1D 02717, very quickly, sir. This is from Halilovic. It's dated 23 September 1993, and it begins by saying: "At the time of saving Mostar from the Ustasha rampage our forces -- our forces' combat operation in the general Vrdi village area facing Mostar are the most important on the BH front." Have you had a chance to look at this particular judgement, and could you please tell us where the Vrdi front is?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this document before. Vrdi is an elevation midway between Jablanica and Mostar, roughly speaking, but belonging to Mostar municipality. About 20 kilometres away from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: All right. And if you could look at number 4, and if you go -- if you are able to help us out. Put on your glasses, sir, and then look at number 4.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and are you able to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My comment is the following: At the time I was a prisoner with Zuka in Doljani-Jablanica, and this is what is mentioned in paragraph 4 of this document. In a way, I was helping with the implementation of this order in the following way: I and other prisoners had to load the cannons and other kinds of weapons for this planned attack on the Vrdi elevation. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: All right. The next document is 1D 03039, and I just need confirmation. This is a document that you provided to us when you arrived at The Hague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: The next document is 1D 02243. This is a brief chronology, and as I understand it, you are familiar with this document, and could you please tell us to what extent you are or why are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document, the reason being I was myself involved in terms of helping a team of Tribunal investigators between 1995 and 1998. At their request I sought out potential witnesses. I tracked them down for them, people they could talk to. Between 1995 and late 1998, the teams visited Mostar over 20 times. I remember some names. Mr. Tom Kempenaars, representative of The Hague Tribunal based in Zagreb. He's the one who announced this particular visit in May 1995, and then in September 1995, there was Mr. Regis Abribat who headed the investigation team. Sometime late in 1997 they completed their investigation. They thanked us, and they said that there was now sufficient circumstantial evidence, information, and indications for indictments to be raised against at least 13 persons. They were followed by a new team including some of the investigators involved in the previous team. I remember the names, and the team was headed by Mr. Nikolai Mihajlov. They worked into 1998 and I worked for about six months. However, as far as that investigation was concerned, there was never an indictment that was raised here before this Tribunal or before any of the national courts. I believe that sufficiently explains the document.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what did you -- did you write any of this report and, if so, what part? We don't need any of the details.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I, too, contributed to this report, especially as concerned information about Jablanica and Konjic, since that was an area that I was familiar with.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: And finally the very last document which is 1D 03040. Again this is a document that you provided to us, and if you could just confirm that and then tell us what the document is. Where did you get it from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I confirm that I gave you this document. I got it from the International Red Cross to confirm that I was registered by them in the museum camp in Jablanica after I returned from my previous two locations Donja Jablanica and Mostar. International Red Cross registered me after I had already spent three months at the museum camp.

utterances.speaker: THE PANEL MENTIONED IN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This concludes my direct examination. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. The best is to break now for 20 minutes. After this break we shall resume with the cross-examinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Ms. Nozica, there's a brief oral decision on follow-up of what I said about the number of documents. The oral decision has to do with the list of exhibits which will be presented when Neven Tomic will appear as a witness. On the 13th October 2008, Prlic's Defence disclosed the of lists of exhibits which it intends to show to Neven Tomic as a witness according to the last schedule by Prlic Defence. Neven Tomic is to appear as from 27 October 2008 and Prlic's Defence wishes to have six hours for its direct examination. Chamber notes the list furnished by Defence has more than 370 documents exactly 373. The Chamber reminds the parties that they have managed to present maximum of 80 exhibits roughly during examination of six hours. Therefore, the Chamber orders Prlic Defence to sort out those documents and to present a list which will contain a reasonable number of documents to be examined during the hearing through Neven Tomic as a witness so that the Prosecution may prepare its cross-examination in an adequate manner. So that's what I told you, Mr. Karnavas, yesterday, and this follows what we have said yesterday. Now, for the cross-examination I understood that Ms. Nozica will have one hour roughly, and it seems to me that Mr. Vasic or Mr. Praljak will need a few minutes also. That's what I understood. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we shall have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will have a number of questions for this witness. I talked to my learned friend Ms. Nozica, and I -- I do know that the other Defence teams will not have any questions, so Ms. Nozica and I will divide our time equally for the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, one hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon. I have distributed my documents, and before I start my cross I would like to inform the Chamber that my examination will be a cross-examination about subjects raised in chief. We want to make sure we don't waste any time on objections. There are some questions, but I'm entirely in the hands of the Court. If the Court believes at the close of my cross-examination that some of the topics were outside the framework, I'm perfectly prepared for the possibility that the Chamber will take away some of the time that was allocated to the Stojic Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note could all the other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My name is Senka Nozica, and I defend Mr. Bruno Stojic. As you've just heard, I will be asking you some questions. We'll be using some documents. The documents have been distributed. This is a binder of documents that you haven't seen before, but we shall be discussing subjects that you are familiar with. Nonetheless, before we move on, yesterday during your examination-in-chief by my learned friend Mr. Karnavas you were asked about a meeting that you attended with Mr. Izetbegovic. That was followed by a succession of objections. You did not provide an answer, but the transcript recorded the question that you were asked. Can you please now explain what sort of a meeting that was? How did Mr. Izetbegovic happen to be there, and what exactly happened at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was invited to come to the Jablanica hydroelectric plant, a plant that produces electricity. They said that Mr. Izetbegovic would be at the meeting too. I came to the meeting, and I realised that all -- all the leaders from the political life and from the local economy in the Jablanica area were there. I looked around. I realised that I was the only Croat there, but that didn't seem to matter. Following Mr. Izetbegovic's arrival, the hosts informed him briefly about the political, security related, and economic questions of any note in the Jablanica area. After that, Mr. Izetbegovic asked the manager of the hydroelectric plant, Muharem Tanovic the following question: "Manager, sir, if necessary, do you think we could cut off the electricity supply for Herceg-Bosna?" And manager Tanovic replied, "That can be done, President, sir." And then Izetbegovic said, "Well, that is a good thing." That's as much as I can tell you about the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You've told us everything, Mr. Zelenika, but you don't give us the time-frame. When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in the fall of 1992. I can't be more specific. It wasn't wintertime. It wasn't summertime. It was the fall of 1992. It might have been October, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember, if you have any knowledge, that, in fact, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina after that period and until the end of the war used electricity as a weapon, as a means of pressuring the population or some of the areas inhabited by Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have knowledge about that. After I was -- after I got out of the camp of the -- on the 1st of March, 1994, I found out that in Mostar there was no power either. And my wife had worked for 13 years in the electrical company, and she knew certain things about the technology. Although she was a lawyer, she knew that there was a plant in Jablanica where the electricity, not only from the power station in Jablanica but also other power stations, could be redirected. That's one piece of information. Another piece of information is that just after the conflict, the armed conflict between the HVO and the BH army on the 15th of April, the electricity in the western part of Jablanica municipality, in the area held by the HVO, was turned off on that day, and for the following 22 months people had no electricity, although the armed conflict between the HVO and the BH army did not last that long. In the summer of 1994, when I had recovered a bit, I came to Jablanica to the first meetings organised by international mediators between the warring parties so that they could start a dialogue, and at the very first meeting, I raised the issue of electricity, supply to the western part of our municipality which was mainly inhabited by Croats. I raised the issue at least three times in that period. And when I realised there is no willingness to deal with the issue, then we in the area inhabited by Croats had to make a move of our own and build a new transmission line to bring electricity from a different power station, whereas until that time we had used electricity from the Jablanica power station.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's very clear. I just have to make a pause between question and answer to make sure that everything is on the record, because we speak the same language, and we must not overlap. Thank you very much for this answer. We'll now move on to another topic, and we'll come back to the documents about the use and abuse of electricity. I will call 1D 01461, and you will see that document on the screen. You have been shown that document before by Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, that's from the batch of Mr. Karnavas under 8, civilian authorities in Jablanica. It's document number 6. I'm sorry I hadn't prepared it again, because it was used today.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to ask you for a comment on this document. Let us focus just on that first paragraph, which will introduce my further questions. It's a document from the Presidency of the Jablanica municipality, signed by Nijaz Ivkovic, and as my colleague Mr. Karnavas said, was the 12th January, and the first paragraph reads: "The media (BH radio and TV) have lately broadcast information depicting Jablanica municipality and the situation in it in a very tendentious and malicious way causing concern and fear among the citizens of Jablanica and its legal bodies." You were asked a question by Mr. Karnavas about this. There is talk here of violence and incidents that occurred up until the 12th of January. There is something that I would like us to be more specific about, though. If you look at the parentheses, it says that the information was broadcast by the BH radio and TV. Can you tell me under whose control the BH TV was at the time and I believe you know that. Where was it physically located and under whose control was it, both the radio and the television?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the BH radio and the BH TV were in Sarajevo, and were under the control of the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Or the BH army; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we therefore conclude that the BH TV that was under the control of the BH army was broadcasting news, criticising action taken by the BH army in the Jablanica area?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. I object to both the leading nature of the question and also to the speculation. There's no -- there's no indication on the record at this point this witness knows who was operating the radio station. Counsel's questions were where was it located. It may have been located in territory then controlled in general, one might say, by Muslim forces, but to jump from -- ask this witness to jump from that to that they were operating and broadcasting these whatever broadcast, shows, whatever you want to call it, is a huge jump of logic and the witness can't say that unless he can indicate he has some personal knowledge of it. I don't think he's given any indication that he was in Sarajevo at these radio stations or television stations at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just respond briefly? First of all, I would like to inform my learned friend that this is a cross-examination. I'm allowed to ask leading questions. Secondly, I assume that all of us in this courtroom know that Sarajevo, throughout the war between that April and the signing of the Dayton agreement was under the control of the Serbs in the middle of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are generally known facts. I asked the witness to confirm that, and I asked him to tell me how he knows that. Both the BH TV and the BH radio were in Sarajevo throughout the war. He confirmed that he knew this. I asked him whether he knew. He said he did. That is generally known fact, and throughout they were under the control of the BH army. This is a generally known fact. I will allow the witness to say how he came to know that, and he will explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a single correction for the transcript. Lines 18 and 19, Ms. Nozica said that throughout the period, she specified Sarajevo was surrounded by the Serbs but under the control of the BH army. May that be clarified, please lest the misinterpretation lead to some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you heard the question. You heard the objection. You heard the reply. The question is as follows: Did the Sarajevo BiH radio, was it under the BiH control in Sarajevo? That was the question put to you. And in answering a question -- or TV, rather. And in answering a question you said that there was cable TV in Jablanica and that you could receive Sarajevo programmes in that way. Did I understand properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I am taking issue with you, Ms. Nozica, about cross-examination. Mr. Karnavas has announced that in his direct, he would cover the question of this electricity plan. Then he had -- his time was up, and electricity did not come in his direct. Now, I find it difficult to accept -- and you have indicated that you would leave it to the Chamber anyhow, that it is cross-examination when, in fact, you continue the direct on a subject which was announced as a subject on direct but was not -- was not mentioned in direct. I think it's rather a continuation. So I think also it would be correct that you would refrain from direct questions on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this caution, Your Honour. I have completed the Izetbegovic meeting, and now I've moved on to an entirely new subject, but I do agree with you. If you believe that the Izetbegovic meeting is examination-in-chief, deduct the time from the time allocated to me. I'm entirely in your hands. I am now moving on to a document that the witness has been shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and I'm much relieved now that we have harmony in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, sir, I would like us to return to this because I considered this to be exceptionally important. Judge Antonetti asked you a while ago whether there was any sort of capable TV in Konjic -- rather in Jablanica, and you said yes. Can I ask you one thing about this document, what exactly does it say here? Is there a reference here to something? Is there a specific reference here to BH radio and TV? My question was where was the headquarters, and then my learned friend the Prosecutor stepped in to say how can you possibly know that, and can you please just answer this: Was Sarajevo the seat of both the BH TV and the BH radio, and how did you come to know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH TV and radio were headquartered in Sarajevo. How do I know that? The distance between Jablanica and Sarajevo is a mere 72 kilometres. Therefore, it's not exactly the far end of the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's move on. Was it the same way before the war? Were both the BH TV and the BH radio headquartered in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Could you just very briefly explain to the Chamber how you know that between April and the Dayton agreement that Sarajevo was encircled on the one hand and under the control of the BH army on the other?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because I was receiving information from the -- both TV and radio. I received their information.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now we built the foundation, and now I'm going back to the document. Would the document not seem to suggest that it was that TV station and that radio station under the control of the BH army were being critical about what the armed forces or some elements of the BH army were doing in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The problem here is that the local authorities in Jablanica in no way agreed with the information such as it was being transmitted by these two media because the information tended to be biased, tended to be untrue and never reflected the situation as it was. Hence the need for an announcement or a statement like this. It was read on many occasions over the local cable TV in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you now go back to the first document in my binder. It is 2D 01431. You know about the Herceg Stjepan brigade, the Mijat Tomic, the battalion, and this report was signed by Marko Zelenika. Do you know Marko Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. The date is the 11th of November, 1992. Now I'll just remind you of a couple of important points reflected in this report about the situation as it prevailed in Jablanica at the time. And you can tell us what you know about that. It reads: "After the events in Prozor, the BH armed forces in Jablanica have begun with activities causing unrest and disturbance with the Croatian population." And then you go on to list some of these such as placing granite blocks on the road between Jablanica and Prozor in a place called Slatina. Can you confirm that this was, in fact, the case back in November, on or about the 11th of November that these activities were in process?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It goes on to state: "In Slatina they are digging trenches, setting up machine-gun nests and deploying themselves at these positions about 50 to 60 soldiers." It goes on: "As a consequence of these activities, some of the Croatian population is moving out of the area, because they are being taunted, firing near their houses, verbal abuse, threats and other things." Did you know about this too?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can fully confirm this as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Okay. It goes on to say: "On the road from Jablanica towards Doljani, three rows of granite blocks were set up, and after we threatened to move all the Croats out of Jablanica, they removed those." Can you confirm that too?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "On the way into Doljani, along the Jablanica road, machine-gun nests are being built that they are still holding." Did you have this information?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually saw this myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In the town of Jablanica, they are setting up multiple machine-gun nests on top of buildings. The museum, the Unis building, two residential buildings, the hill facing the building in which the HVO command is located, the railway station, and other positions too. Can you remember if you saw any of these?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some I did. But I can confirm what you're talking about in terms of this being the general context.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: They are moving municipal workers out. You should know that is true. And they're turning the building into an armed forces military base or, rather, the command of the Neretva Brigade. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that in detail. There's an order from the War Presidency for the hydroelectric plant admin to be moved out of the old hotel and the municipal administration would now be moving into the old hotel, whereas the previous building of the administration would be now turned into a barracks to be used by the 44th Neretva Mountain Brigade in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. I just between draw your attention to something else, and this is the second to last paragraph on the is second to last paragraph of this document in Croatian it reads: "We were drawing their attention to the fact that all the newly set up machine-guns were trained on Croat settlements and that they had to remove those. This came to nothing, however. Quite the contrary, in fact. They are setting up new machine-gun nests." Was this the situation that you found in November, and can you confirm that the same situation continued in December as well, these acts of provocation by the BH army throughout the period were a permanent feature?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that in its entirety. As time went on, the whole thing was being stepped up little by little.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas asked you about how the political leadership was replaced in Konjic, and you spoke about that a little. I will show you another document now. I'm not sure if you've seen it before but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to another document. This document is signed by Marko Zelenika. Is that your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was part of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade, 3rd Battalion, 11th of November, 1992. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was the commander of the battalion that was part of the Herceg Stjepan brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was your brother detained with you in the museum? This morning we saw a list, and he was in the list as you were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he was detained in Donja Jablanica with Zuka, and then because of the consequences he suffered he died in a camp. He was not at the museum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he die because of the consequences of his detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what the doctors established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that either. I wouldn't have tried to summon these emotions in you. I wasn't aware of the fact that this was your brother. Sir, perhaps you want another break.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no need.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, can we move on to our next document in this binder? I'm not sure if you've seen it or not. This is 2D 000814. Have you found the document, sir? This is an order by Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You've never seen this one before?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. I'll do my best to tell you in a nutshell what it's about. Let's see if these are incidents that you, too, you familiar with. I'm talking about incidents or developments in which the BH army leadership and the SDA leadership appointed Mr. Cibo and others in Jablanica because they were unhappy with the policies in Jablanica and Konjic, the policies pursued by individuals who were working with the Croatian population. And then in the preamble this is addressed. It tells us about information being available, that in the Jablanica, Konjic, Pozrica, Pazajevina [as interpreted] area and probably other areas too. Throughout the area responsibility of the 4th Corps, a minor part of BH army personnel of the MUP and of the authorities, are now entirely in the service of the HZ HB. And then there is particular focus on Dr. Hadzihusejnovic from Konjic and others too, and then comes the order. "Go to Igman as soon as possible. Have a talk with the Igman OG commander, Dzevad Radja, and Zulfikar Alispago as well as others. Number two, enlist the assistance of all the other sources in order to be able to take in the entire situation. The problem as follows deal with anything that is in your purview, make any replacements that you need. Paragraph 4 says: "Propose special measures, prosecute if need be, and take any other steps that you deem necessary." And then paragraph 5 says: "Check if similar things are going on elsewhere." Mr. Zelenika, can you confirm that this order reflects precisely what you have been telling us about. And what I mean is the efforts made by the BH army leadership to sever any links that may have existed between the HVO, the civilian authorities in Jablanica Konjic and other localities on the one hand, and the BH army and the civilian authorities as they refer to themselves of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the other.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way this is a blueprint for what happened at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Excellent. Can we now please move on to page 2 of this document. I will read this out to you slowly. The 22nd of January, 1993. The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, same as the one before. 1st Corps command. It reads -- this is to the Jablanica command, specifically commander Safet Bozo. "Safet, you should go to Konjic and convey a serious warning to Jasmin Guska of the Konjic police because of his cooperation with the HVO and giving away the BH army positions. He should be seriously threatened because we are receiving daily reports on his actions. Tell him that the BH army military security has authorised you to give him this final warning. "Regards, the Doctor." Who was referred to as the Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the second document that we're looking at today that confirms the authority of the Dr. Safet Cibo to get involved in military matters. As for this man Safet, his name is Hindic his nickname is Bozo. He is a commander of the military police from Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll certainly defer to the language experts on this I only raise it -- the possibility, but at least as it's translated in the English version of that particular document, what is says is this man should be seriously reprimanded as opposed to threatened, which was the question that counsel put to the witness. She used the word threatened. Again if it's a language issue, I will defer to the experts on that but document says reprimanded not threatened and I note there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to confirm that the word used in the original is threatened as opposed to reprimanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have reprimanded in English. I hear from the French booth that the word as translated was mis en garde, so warning, or cautioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the mistake is mine. This is an OTP exhibit used in a different trial, and it was admitted in this form. This is an OTP translation, and I'm quite happy that the Prosecutor was the one to notice the error. The original reads zaprijetiti. The document was provided to the booths, and they can deal with this. After all, we have it in e-court as well. It reads he should be seriously threatened, not cautioned or warned. I'm not sure if clarifies it. Can we take this to have been corrected now and the record set straight. My colleagues believe that I should repeat this. The original reads "He should be seriously threatened." We have this in e-court, the original, and the interpreters, too, can see that this is indeed what the original says. Is this clear now? May I move on?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Another thing that is noteworthy, and I do have to go back to this because we've been slightly derailed by this interpretation discussion, but just to make this clear to myself. Can you confirm that this document was signed by "the doctor," the doctor being Safet Cibo?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Something else we've looked at the documents shown to you by Mr. Karnavas about Mr. Cibo's appointment to a certain military position in March 1993, the 20th of March, and then Mr. Izetbegovic appointed him on the 13th of March to that civilian position as president of the War Presidency, chairman of the War Presidency. We see him taking steps as early as January 1993 in the Konjic and Jablanica areas because that's what we're talking about, these two areas; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I would like to go a little step -- no. I -- I had been looking for the signature, and now I see that it is on the very first -- on the -- on the first paper, think. There is actually a signature, because in the translation it says also. I'm sorry. That is Halilovic, but you asked about the signature of Cibo, and the witness said yes, but we just see the name "The Doctor." So I suppose your question is whether he can say that "The Doctor" stands for Mr. Cibo, and then I think we should perhaps know how he can conclude this. Witness, now -- there is no signature of Dr. Cibo in these documents. You agree? You --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You said there was one and you recognise it. But how can you tell us that it is -- that the term "Doctor" hides Dr. Cibo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Cibo was, as a matter of fact, a doctor. So in Jablanica and Konjic, whenever somebody said "The doctor," we knew there was a reference to Mr. Safet Cibo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So he was the only one there, the only doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. He was the only doctor who was in a position of authority, both the civilian authority and interfering with the work of the military units. There were other doctors around, but they did no such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Maybe it was a slip of the tongue. I didn't mention that. I just asked about who the person was. I know there is a no signature. I can see for myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, can we move on to the next. This is document P 01696, and we'll just skim through this document. This is an order that you were shown by Mr. Karnavas. This is Prlic Defence document 1D 2756. We see here that Dr. Cibo was then appointed to a military position, right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We realise now that he had an appointment to one of the civilian bodies chairman of the Crisis Staff by Mr. Izetbegovic. And then again for the benefit of the transcript, the document is 1D 2753. Now, sir, let us move on to 2D 01439. This is a document from Konjic. The date is, and that's an important date for me, the 12th of April, 1993. The Herceg Stjepan Brigade from Konjic. You tell us yourself that the distance between Jablanica and Konjic is very small. Can you also confirm that the towns had a lot of links during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's go to paragraph 3. On April 10th and 11th, and this is in 1993, of this year, representatives of the BH Ministry of Interior Avdo Hebib and Nijaz Skenderagic were in Konjic, their objective being to relieve from duty the president of the wartime Presidency Dr. Rusmir Hadzihusejnovic on behalf of the RBH Presidency. The task was done on the 11th of April at 11 o'clock in the presence of Esad Ramic, and this was something that was done by the state commission on behalf of the 4th BH army corps. As a result, as of the 10th of April Safet Cibo became the official president of Konjic -- wartime president of Konjic municipality. Do you remember if this really happened, because when you testified in-chief, you said you knew that Dr. Hadzihusejnovic did not just leave his position without putting up a fight. Is this the event that you discussed, where there was a certain, what shall I put, an abuse of force in order to make this man leave this post?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really glad because this document seems to confirm what I testified to in chief. I've never seen this document that much is true but this is exactly the information that was available to me and what my information indicated, and that was the interpretation I offered in chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we look -- we'll go through the next documents quickly. The next one is 2D 00237. You had said at the beginning of my examination and in the course of the examination-in-chief that the conflict between the HVO and the BH army occurred on the 15th of April, 1993. I'll show you a couple of documents that reflect this situation. This is a document from Jablanica signed by the commander of the 5th Battalion, Stipe Pole. Did you know Stipe Pole?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is the report of the 12th of March. Mr. Pole says in item 1 as follows: "After the removal the flag from the installation where the military police was stationed (currently moved to Doljani) at 1500 hours possession of the rooms used by the BH army military police was taken by force." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Jablanica then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Number 2: "Zulfikar Alispago, Zuka, settled with his unit at the Jablanica hotel." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Item 3: "Beginning with 1500 hours, check-points performed in intensified control and search of Croat nationals." Do you remember these activities?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have personal experience. When I went to Mostar on the 13th, I was turned back from the check-point near Aleksin Han. So as early as the 13th, I was unable to go Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next time -- item says that Dr. Safet Cibo prohibited all catering establishments from remaining open after 1500 hours. Do you remember measures of this kind?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says, "As we speak, the vehicles of Zuka's army circled around town and more intense shooting occurred around the Jablanica water turbine."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I lived 30, 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now look at P 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a little correction. You have said that the document was of the 12th of March, but in my copy it says April, and I think also in the original it is corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's a slip of the tongue maybe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document is P 1882, dated 15 April 1993. Again signed by Stipe Pole, Herceg Stjepan brigade, 3rd Battalion, Mijat Tomic, Jablanica. Third line from the top. Muslim forces are carrying out movements and maneuvers in order to encircle our forces in Sovici and Doljani. Any and every entrance or exits of citizens of the Croat nationality into and from the city is prohibited, so that 600 of our civilians remain in the city. From the territory of our municipality there are ongoing operations in the Neretvica valley, the strongest oppositions are being carried out from the direction of Ostrozac Muslim forces are moving from Paprasko across the lake towards Boksevica. In your evidence you said yourself that two days earlier you were unable to go to Mostar, you were prevented from leaving the city. This document confirms this, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the 600 civilians who remained in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document. P 1977. You spoke during examination-in-chief about a meeting that you attended personally on the 12th of June, 1993, chaired by Mr. Cibo.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report from Rama Prozor, IPD, information and propaganda section, dated 19 April 1993. I'll show you just one segment that you might know about. Was there a report on that -- at that meeting about looting by committed BH army members against Croats and other incidents victimizing Croats? This passage that's the fourth paragraph says: "In the areas held by Muslim extremists, Croat homes are being looted and torched, whereas the population is being captured and taken no one knows where. In Jablanica itself they are expelling Croats from their homes, mistreating them and expelling them from Jablanica, trying in that way to ethnically cleanse Jablanica and deliver it to Sefer and his associates." And then it goes on to say: "In the afternoon of the 18 April 1993, they disconnected electricity to Rama Prozor." Can you confirm that this happened at that time? Does this document faithfully reflect also what was discussed at that meeting, what you said to Mr. Cibo on the 12th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not listed in the order of the seriousness of -- of crimes, because it's a much graver offence to take someone prisoner than to seize their car. But it does mention the cut-off of electricity and the blackout, the resulting blackout lasted for 22 months, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You are trying to say that if you had written the report yourself, you would have put capturing people first, then expelling people from their apartments, and then, perhaps, I would have mentioned cars. But for the rest you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's see document 2D 01143. It reflects precisely what you said at the meeting of the 12th of June, 1993. It's report by SIS from 1995 to be quite clear, but it speaks of the destruction of buildings in the territory of Jablanica municipalities, and then it mentions April and May, and it says: "Members of the BH army devastated in villages Zuglici, Mrakovo, and Sabancici, 20 residential buildings owned by Croats. Croats from these villages were first expelled to Jablanica, and not long afterwards, they were imprisoned at the museum prison." Then it refers again to looting. "In Orasac five Croat homes were looted. In Jablanica one Croat house was looted. And Croat families were driven out of 50 apartments. In Doljani a unit of the BH army entered the hamlets listed here. In Doljani itself members of the BH army looted and destroyed the community house, the community hall. In Slatina 20 houses were looted and burnt down." We have a list of other villages where this happened, and churches and cemeteries near Jablanica, Doljani, Globusica damaged in this same period. Having looked at this document, can you confirm most of these incidents? Were you aware of all that at the time or learned about it later?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about that. Already in the second half of April 1993 members of the BH army in Zuglici, Mrakovo, Sabancici, and Donja Jablanica villages took away all the Croats living there, brought them to the intersection in Jablanica outside the hotel and left them to their own devices. Some of the Croats went to the homes of the family they had in Jablanica, but they were later picked up and put in prison together with the others. In Jablanica, in the six, seven Croat homes, the people were expelled, and Zuka's army moved then to the hotel making it its base. From that time on the hotel was called Zuka's base. We called it the Rogic houses or Zuka's base.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we look at P 2128. You will see that it's a manuscript. It's best a code-name Ognja. That's the name of the author. It's sent to the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of BH. It says to be urgently submitted to the chief of the Main Staff. It says Maxum Salim [phoen] to all, especially Mr. Ognjak. I suppose you don't know who Ognja is either, but let us look at something very important in this document. It begins on page 3, in the Croat version, and in English that would be 00430013. I will focus on 00430015. That's the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. My apologies. [French on English channel] Your Honour, before this document was put before the witness for -- well, questions and answers, could we get some indication of the source of this document? It's a handwritten document. There's no indication of where it comes from, and I would ask counsel to at least give us some preliminary indication of the authenticity of this document, where it was -- where it was obtained.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect for my learned friend from the Prosecution, I have to say that since this is a Prosecution document, these questions he should be able to answer himself.
